title: Defensive Shape Foundations
primarySkill: Establishing a connected defensive shape behind the ball.
objective: Develop players’ ability to form, maintain and adjust a compact defensive shape as the football moves across the ground.
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a rectangular playing area with a target gate at each end.
Divide players into an attacking team and a defending team.
Begin with the attacking team holding possession at one end.
Position the defenders between the football and the opposite target gate.
The attacking team moves the football by kick or handball but initially does not attempt to score.
Defenders are restricted to shadow pressure during the first phase.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team circulates the football across and through the area.
Defenders move as a connected unit, maintaining appropriate width, depth and spacing.
When the football moves laterally, the defensive group slides together rather than chasing individually.
The nearest defender applies controlled pressure while teammates protect central and deeper space.
The coach occasionally calls “freeze” and checks the location, spacing and body position of each defender.
After five successful attacking possessions, the attacking team attempts to move the football through the target gate.
Defenders score one point for forcing the attack backwards, wide or into a turnover.
Teams rotate roles after two minutes.
coachingPoints: Maintain a compact shape between the football and the scoring target.
Move when the football moves rather than reacting after the receiver has taken possession.
The nearest defender presses while the next defenders provide cover.
Protect the corridor and force the attack towards wider, less dangerous areas.
Maintain enough spacing to cover ground without creating large gaps.
Communicate the location of opponents, space and possible switches.
Defenders behind the play must scan both the football and their direct opponent.
Reset the shape immediately after every disposal.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders move together or as disconnected individuals.
Whether the nearest defender applies pressure without opening central space.
Whether deeper defenders remain goal-side.
Whether players communicate before the football arrives.
Whether the defensive line becomes too flat or too stretched.
How quickly the group resets after the football changes direction.

commonErrors.error: Defenders chase the football individually.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce that one player pressures while the rest protect space and maintain connection.

commonErrors.error: Large gaps appear between defenders.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the area temporarily and set a maximum spacing of 8–10 metres.

commonErrors.error: Defenders watch only the football.
commonErrors.correction: Require players to regularly point to or name their direct opponent.

commonErrors.error: The corridor is left open.
commonErrors.correction: Position the deepest defender centrally and ask the group to force play wide.

progressions: Allow attackers to score immediately through either target gate.
Add an attacking player who begins behind the defensive line.
Introduce live intercepts and controlled tackling.
Award double points for an attacking score through the corridor.
Begin each repetition from a turnover so defenders must recover into shape.
regressions: Use handball only to slow the movement of the football.
Mark defensive reference zones with cones.
Allow the coach to stop play frequently and physically reposition players.
successIndicators: Maintain connected spacing as the football moves.
Protect the corridor before pressuring wide possession.
Identify the pressure, cover and deeper-defender roles.
Communicate early and clearly.
Reset their shape within two to three seconds of each disposal.
matchApplication: This drill introduces the basic team-defence shape required when the opposition controls possession. It teaches defenders to protect dangerous central space, support the player applying pressure and prevent one disposal from breaking the entire defensive structure.

title: Goal-Side Positioning Fundamentals
primarySkill: Maintaining goal-side positioning against an opponent.
objective: Teach defenders to remain between their opponent and the scoring target while still applying effective pressure to the football.
equipment: 1 scoring gate or pair of portable goals
coachingDifficulty: 2 – Basic coaching knowledge and one main teaching point
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with a scoring gate at one end.
Pair each attacker with a defender.
Position attackers between 15 and 25 metres from the scoring gate.
Begin with a feeder holding the football outside the area.
Defenders start one to two metres from their opponent in a goal-side position.
The first phase is non-contact apart from controlled body positioning.
howTheDrillWorks:
Attackers move within the area attempting to create separation from their defender.
Defenders track their opponent while staying between the opponent and the scoring gate.
The feeder selects an attacker and delivers the football by kick or handball.
The defender attempts to spoil, intercept or force the attacker away from the scoring gate.
If the attacker gains possession, they have five seconds to score through the gate.
Defenders score one point for maintaining goal-side position and forcing the attacker away from goal.
They score two points for an intercept or clean spoil.
Rotate the feeder and swap attacking and defensive roles after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Begin in a position that protects the scoring side of the opponent.
Keep the hips and shoulders open enough to see both the football and the opponent.
Adjust the distance from the opponent according to the position of the football.
Close space as the feeder prepares to dispose of the football.
Avoid standing directly behind the opponent where movement cannot be seen.
Use small adjustment steps rather than crossing the feet.
Recover goal-side immediately if the opponent gains separation.
Communicate when another defender may need to switch or assist.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders begin between their opponent and the scoring target.
Whether defenders can see both the opponent and the football.
Whether defenders close space at the correct time.
Whether players lose balance by crossing their feet.
Whether beaten defenders recover through the inside rather than chasing from behind.
Whether defenders force attackers towards less dangerous space.

commonErrors.error: Defender stands directly behind the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Move to a slightly angled position that allows vision of both the opponent and the football.

commonErrors.error: Defender overcommits towards the feeder.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce that protecting the scoring side is the first responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Defender reacts only after the kick is released.
commonErrors.correction: Ask the defender to read the feeder’s preparation and close space before the disposal.

commonErrors.error: Recovery run goes outside the attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the defender to recover through the shortest inside line towards goal.

progressions: Allow attackers to lead in any direction before turning towards goal.
Add a second attacker and defender to create potential switches.
Permit full live contests and legal tackling.
Use a kick rather than a handball from the feeder.
Introduce a second scoring gate to increase scanning demands.
regressions: Restrict attackers to one nominated leading direction.
Reduce the size of the area.
Allow defenders to begin closer to their opponent.
successIndicators: Remain between their opponent and the scoring target.
See both the football and their direct opponent.
Close space as the disposal is prepared.
Force possession away from the central scoring line.
Recover goal-side quickly when initially beaten.
matchApplication: Goal-side positioning is essential when defending leading forwards, midfielders pushing inside 50 and opponents spreading from stoppages. The drill teaches defenders to protect the most dangerous route to goal before attempting to win possession.

title: Corridor Protection Gate
primarySkill: Protecting the corridor and forcing opposition possession wide.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to deny central ball movement and guide the opposition towards wider, less dangerous areas.
groundSize: 45 metres long × 40 metres wide, with a central corridor 12 metres wide.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular playing area.
Use cones to create a 12-metre-wide corridor through the centre.
Place one scoring gate at the end of the corridor and two wider scoring gates near the boundaries.
Divide players into attackers and defenders.
The attacking team starts with possession at one end.
Defenders begin in a compact shape protecting the central gate.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to move the football through any scoring gate.
A score through the central gate is worth three points.
A score through a wide gate is worth one point.
The defending team applies angled pressure designed to close the corridor and guide possession wide.
The nearest defender pressures the ball carrier while teammates close central passing lanes.
Defenders score two points for an intercept and one point for forcing a turnover outside the corridor.
After a turnover, the defending team has five seconds to move the football back through the starting line.
Teams swap roles after three minutes.
coachingPoints: Protect the central gate before applying pressure to wide possession.
Approach the ball carrier on an angle that removes the inside option.
The second defender must protect the next central receiver.
Keep the deepest defender aligned with the corridor.
Do not overcollapse towards the football and leave the opposite side completely open.
Communicate when the football is likely to switch.
Adjust the team shape early as the ball carrier prepares to dispose of the football.
Force high, slow or difficult kicks towards the boundary.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether pressure is applied from the correct angle.
Whether the corridor is protected by more than one defensive layer.
Whether defenders become attracted to wide possession unnecessarily.
Whether the deepest defender remains centrally positioned.
Whether the weak-side defenders scan and adjust.
Whether turnovers are created in predictable wide areas.

commonErrors.error: Defender approaches straight at the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Angle the approach from inside to outside and remove the corridor option.

commonErrors.error: Too many defenders chase wide possession.
commonErrors.correction: Nominate one pressure defender and keep the remaining players connected centrally.

commonErrors.error: Weak-side space is left unprotected.
commonErrors.correction: Require the weak-side defender to slide to a central cover position.

commonErrors.error: Defenders retreat without applying pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Balance corridor protection with active pressure on the ball carrier.

progressions: Reduce the width of the defensive corridor.
Allow attackers to run and carry before disposing.
Introduce full tackling.
Award attackers five points for a corridor score.
Start the drill from different field positions, including half-back and the wing.
regressions: Increase the width of the corridor.
Allow the defence to begin set before each repetition.
successIndicators: Deny direct central movement.
Apply pressure from an inside-out angle.
Maintain cover behind the pressing defender.
Force the opposition to use wider, slower routes.
Create turnovers near the boundary or outside the corridor.
matchApplication: The drill replicates defending opposition ball movement from defensive 50, through the centre square or into attacking 50. It teaches the team to remove the shortest path to goal and force possession into less dangerous areas.

title: Crossing Leads Defensive Handover
primarySkill: Handing over opponents when attacking leads cross.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to communicate and exchange opponents when crossing leads make it inefficient or unsafe to remain with the original match-up.
equipment: 1 scoring gate or set of goals
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a forward-entry area with a feeder positioned 25–35 metres from goal.
Place two attackers and two defenders inside the area.
Attackers begin on opposite sides and prepare to make crossing leads.
Defenders begin goal-side and slightly inside their direct opponents.
Use additional pairs in separate grids where numbers allow.
Begin with predetermined leads before introducing choice.
howTheDrillWorks:
On the feeder’s movement, both attackers lead and cross through the centre of the area.
Defenders decide whether to remain with their original opponent or complete a handover.
A handover must include an early verbal call and clear visual confirmation.
The feeder delivers the football to either attacker.
Defenders attempt to spoil, intercept or force the receiver away from goal.
Attackers score by marking or receiving inside the scoring area.
Defenders score one point for a successful handover and two points for winning possession.
Rotate attackers, defenders and feeders after four repetitions.
coachingPoints: Begin goal-side and protect the central leading lane.
Communicate before the attackers cross, not after separation occurs.
Use clear calls such as “switch”, “stay” and the teammate’s name.
Do not hand over an opponent unless the teammate is positioned to accept responsibility.
Maintain body contact legally through the crossing point.
After a handover, immediately locate the new opponent.
Protect the deeper and more dangerous lead.
Avoid both defenders following the same attacker.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders recognise the crossing pattern early.
Whether the handover call occurs before the attackers separate.
Whether both defenders understand the decision.
Whether the central lane remains protected.
Whether defenders locate the new opponent immediately.
Whether one attacker becomes free because of hesitation.

commonErrors.error: Handover call occurs too late.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate as the attackers approach the crossing point.

commonErrors.error: Both defenders follow the same attacker.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm responsibility with a name and clear “switch” call.

commonErrors.error: Defender accepts a handover from the wrong side.
commonErrors.correction: Remain goal-side and ensure the new opponent cannot lead directly towards goal.

commonErrors.error: Defenders switch automatically every time.
commonErrors.correction: Assess whether staying is safer before committing to a handover.

progressions: Allow attackers to fake the crossing lead.
Add a third attacker and defender.
Permit the feeder to delay or change the disposal.
Introduce full contested marking.
Begin from different forward-entry angles.
regressions: Mark the crossing point with a cone.
Reduce the size of the scoring area.
successIndicators: Recognise crossing leads early.
Make a clear switch-or-stay decision.
Communicate before the handover is required.
Remain goal-side of the new opponent.
Prevent attackers from gaining uncontested central possession.
matchApplication: Forwards regularly cross leads to create defensive confusion and separation. This drill develops the communication and positioning required to hand opponents over without allowing an uncontested mark in a dangerous scoring position.

title: Team Defence Fundamentals Assessment
primarySkill: Applying foundational team-defence principles in an integrated game environment.
objective: Assess whether players can independently apply the foundational team-defence principles introduced in TD-001 to TD-019 during continuous, realistic play.
groundSize: Two-thirds to full ground, depending on player numbers.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two-thirds or the full ground with normal goals at one end.
Divide players into attacking and defending teams.
Position the defence in realistic forward, midfield and deep defensive lines.
Place two wide and two central defensive exit gates.
Prepare a sequence of starting scenarios:
Slow opposition possession
Fast turnover
Wide switch
Outnumbered attack
Forward entry
Failed defensive exit
Assign assistant coaches or leaders to observe specific defensive principles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins each repetition from one of the prepared scenarios.
The attacking team attempts to score using unrestricted football.
The defending team must establish shape, protect dangerous space and apply coordinated pressure.
After a defensive stop, the team attempts to exit through an appropriate gate.
If the exit fails, the coach immediately begins a repeat entry.
Each repetition continues for 45–90 seconds before resetting.
Coaches assess the defence against the nominated success criteria.
Teams swap roles after six repetitions and complete the same scenarios.
coachingPoints: Establish goal-side and central protection immediately.
Maintain connected lines behind the football.
Identify pressure, cover and balance roles around possession.
Force opposition movement towards less dangerous areas.
Communicate opponents, switches, pressure triggers and space behind the play.
Delay when outnumbered and press when support is available.
Reset immediately after failed exits or repeat entries.
Secure possession and select an appropriate defensive exit.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: How quickly the team establishes defensive shape.
Whether defenders remain goal-side.
Whether the corridor and top of defensive 50 are protected.
Whether pressure is supported by cover and balance.
Whether defensive lines remain connected.
Whether communication is early and specific.
Whether the team delays correctly when outnumbered.
Whether players reset after repeat entries.
Whether the first exit decision suits the pressure.
Whether the group adapts without direct coach instruction.

commonErrors.error: Players chase opponents without maintaining team shape.
commonErrors.correction: Re-establish central protection and connected lines before applying aggressive pressure.

commonErrors.error: Pressure occurs without support.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm pressure, cover and balance responsibilities before the next repetition.

commonErrors.error: Defenders remain passive when a clear trigger appears.
commonErrors.correction: Identify the trigger and require the nearest players to press together.

commonErrors.error: The team fails to reset after an unsuccessful exit.
commonErrors.correction: Use an immediate recovery call and rebuild through goal-side positions.

commonErrors.error: Exit decisions are rushed or repeatedly central.
commonErrors.correction: Secure possession, scan and use width when the corridor is congested.

progressions: Remove all coach-directed starting information.
Use full match-like contact.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure scenarios.
Require the defence to transition from the exit into a forward entry.
Allow the attacking team to plan its own method for breaking the defensive structure.
regressions: Assess one defensive principle at a time.
Use half-ground rather than two-thirds or full-ground.
Allow defensive leaders to organise the group before each restart.
successIndicators: Establish a connected shape within three seconds of the starting action.
Protect the corridor and central scoring areas.
Maintain goal-side positioning.
Coordinate pressure, cover and balance.
Communicate across defensive lines.
Delay attacks when outnumbered.
Recognise and act on pressing triggers.
Reset effectively after repeat entries.
Secure the defensive stop and select an appropriate exit.
Apply the principles without constant coach direction.
matchApplication: This assessment combines the foundational team-defence behaviours required in Australian football. It measures whether players can organise collectively, protect dangerous space, respond to changing attacking methods, win possession and transition safely out of defence.
relatedDrills: TD-011 – Pressure, Cover and Balance Rotation

title: Tracking and Releasing a Running Opponent
Sliding Line Against Lateral Ball Movement
Defending the Lead-Up Chain
primarySkill: Defending consecutive lead-up receivers through multiple areas.
objective: Develop coordinated defensive movement against an attack using repeated short leads to advance the football through connected receivers.
groundSize: 55 metres long × 30 metres wide, divided into three sections.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the playing area into three consecutive sections.
Position two attackers and two defenders in each section.
The attacking team begins at one end with the football.
Attackers attempt to advance through a series of short lead-up possessions.
Defenders begin goal-side of their direct opponents.
Place a scoring gate at the far end.
howTheDrillWorks:
An attacker in the first section leads and receives the football.
The defender closes the receiver and attempts to force a backwards or wide disposal.
Attackers in the next section begin their leads as the receiver gains possession.
Defenders communicate whether to track, switch or hand over the next runner.
The attacking team attempts to complete one possession in each section before scoring.
Defenders score one point for forcing a backwards disposal and two points for an intercept or spoil.
After a turnover, defenders attempt to move the football back through the starting line.
Rotate players between sections after each block.
coachingPoints: Close each receiver as the football is arriving.
Protect the inside leading lane.
Defenders behind the football must scan for the next lead before the current disposal.
Communicate runners moving between sections.
Avoid following one opponent so far that the next section becomes exposed.
Recover behind the football after being bypassed.
Use pressure on the receiver to make the next kick predictable.
Maintain connection between defensive sections.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders close receivers before they can turn.
Whether the next lead is identified early.
Whether handovers are communicated.
Whether gaps appear between defensive sections.
Whether beaten defenders recover behind the football.
Whether pressure makes the next disposal predictable.

commonErrors.error: Defender waits until the receiver turns.
commonErrors.correction: Close during the football’s travel and arrive as possession is taken.

commonErrors.error: Defenders watch the current contest only.
commonErrors.correction: Scan forward and identify the next likely receiver.

commonErrors.error: Opponents become free between sections.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate the handover before the runner crosses the section line.

commonErrors.error: Beaten defenders stop participating.
commonErrors.correction: Recover behind the football and support the next defensive action.

progressions: Remove section boundaries.
Allow attackers to run and carry.
Add full legal tackling.
Introduce a wide switch option.
Start from an unpredictable turnover.
regressions: Require attackers to use predetermined receivers.
Allow the coach to pause before each new lead.
successIndicators: Close lead-up receivers before they turn.
Protect inside leading lanes.
Identify the next lead early.
Complete defensive handovers.
Recover and maintain connection behind the football.
matchApplication: Teams often advance through repeated short marks and lead-up targets. This drill teaches defenders to pressure each possession while remaining aware of the next receiver and preserving connection between defensive lines.

title: Defending the Switch Runner
primarySkill: Tracking an opponent who changes from the ball side to the weak side during a switch.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to recognise, track and hand over an opponent moving across the ground during a change in the direction of possession.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the area into left, central and right vertical lanes.
Position attackers across all three lanes.
Match defenders to attackers at the start.
Begin with possession in one outside lane.
Nominate one attacker to run from the ball side across to the weak side as the football is switched.
Place three scoring gates at the far end.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins circulating the football on one side.
A nominated attacker runs behind or through the central lane towards the weak side.
The attack switches the football across the ground.
The original defender tracks the runner until a teammate clearly accepts responsibility.
Weak-side defenders adjust centrally before expanding to the new ball side.
The attackers attempt to use the switch runner to score through a gate.
Defenders score one point for completing the handover and two points for preventing the runner’s possession.
Rotate the switch runner and defensive responsibilities after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Scan for opponents moving away from the original ball side.
Track the runner until responsibility is clearly handed over.
Communicate the runner’s name, lane and direction.
Weak-side defenders must prepare to accept the runner before the switch arrives.
Remain goal-side during the handover.
Avoid both defenders following the runner.
Maintain central protection while adjusting to the new ball side.
Pressure the switch kick to reduce its speed and accuracy.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders scan for the crossing runner.
Whether the original defender maintains responsibility.
Whether the weak-side defender prepares early.
Whether communication is specific and acknowledged.
Whether central space remains protected.
Whether the switch runner receives uncontested possession.

commonErrors.error: Original defender releases the runner too early.
commonErrors.correction: Track until the next defender verbally accepts responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Weak-side defender reacts only after the switch arrives.
commonErrors.correction: Scan and prepare while the football is still on the opposite side.

commonErrors.error: Two defenders follow the same runner.
commonErrors.correction: Complete the handover and require the first defender to return to central cover.

commonErrors.error: Defenders become too wide during the switch.
commonErrors.correction: Protect the corridor before expanding towards the new ball side.

progressions: Add a second crossing runner.
Remove the nominated runner and allow attackers to choose.
Introduce full tackling.
Allow the attack to fake the switch.
Begin from an unpredictable turnover.
regressions: Predetermine the runner and switch direction.
Pause play at the handover point.
successIndicators: Identify runners moving across the ground.
Track until responsibility is transferred.
Complete clear defensive handovers.
Maintain central protection during switches.
Prevent uncontested weak-side possession.
matchApplication: Attacking teams often send runners across the ground during switches to create an extra option on the weak side. Defenders must track and hand over those movements without abandoning the centre of the ground.
relatedDrills: TD-005 – Ball-Side Pressure and Weak-Side Cover
TD-019 – Defensive Shape Through Switch Play

title: Defensive Rotation After a Mark
primarySkill: Reorganising defensive positions while an opponent holds a mark.
objective: Develop players’ ability to use the time created by an opposition mark to reset match-ups, protect dangerous space and prepare for the next phase.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with three attacking gates at one end.
Divide players into attacking and defending teams.
Begin each repetition with an attacker taking an uncontested mark.
Defenders start in deliberately imperfect positions.
The player on the mark must set immediately.
Remaining defenders reorganise while the marked player prepares to dispose.
howTheDrillWorks:
An attacker takes a mark and the nearest defender sets the mark.
The remaining defenders use the pause to identify opponents and dangerous space.
Defenders rotate into goal-side, cover and deeper positions.
The player on the mark attempts to influence the disposal direction without infringing.
After the umpire-style call of “play on”, the attack attempts to score through a gate.
Defenders attempt to force play wide or intercept the next disposal.
Defenders score one point for completing their reset before play resumes and two points for stopping the attack.
Rotate the starting mark position after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Set the mark quickly and legally.
Use the pause to communicate match-ups and loose opponents.
Protect the corridor and deepest space first.
The closest defender picks up the most dangerous free player.
Avoid all defenders moving towards the mark.
Anticipate the likely disposal from the ball carrier’s position and preferred side.
Prepare to move before “play on”.
If the ball carrier plays on, transition immediately into active pressure.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the mark is set quickly.
Whether defenders communicate during the pause.
Whether loose opponents are identified.
Whether central and deeper space is protected.
Whether defenders anticipate the next disposal.
Whether the group reacts immediately when play resumes.

commonErrors.error: Several defenders move towards the player with the mark.
commonErrors.correction: Only the nearest defender sets the mark; others protect opponents and space.

commonErrors.error: Defenders remain silent during the pause.
commonErrors.correction: Use the dead time to identify match-ups and organise the next line.

commonErrors.error: The mark defender allows an easy inside play-on.
commonErrors.correction: Position to discourage the dangerous inside route.

commonErrors.error: Defenders wait for the disposal before moving.
commonErrors.correction: Anticipate the likely option and prepare before play resumes.

progressions: Allow the ball carrier to play on immediately.
Remove the coach’s “play on” call.
Add full tackling after play resumes.
Begin with different field positions.
Add a second consecutive mark requiring another reset.
regressions: Use one central and one wide gate only.
successIndicators: Set the mark quickly.
Use the pause to reorganise.
Identify and cover dangerous opponents.
Protect central and deeper space.
React immediately when play resumes.
matchApplication: An opposition mark provides defenders with a brief opportunity to reset. Teams that use this time effectively can restore match-ups, protect dangerous space and influence the direction of the next disposal.

title: Defensive Front-and-Centre Crumb
primarySkill: Winning or neutralising the front-and-centre position at a marking contest.
objective: Teach defenders to recognise and protect the most dangerous front-and-centre ground-ball area beneath a forward marking contest.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Position a feeder 20–30 metres from a marking contest.
Place one attacker and one defender in the aerial contest.
Position one attacking crumber and one defensive crumber front and centre.
Add one defender goal-side of the contest.
Place a scoring gate behind the contest and two exit gates to either side.
Rotate all players through each role.
howTheDrillWorks:
The feeder kicks to the marking contest.
The aerial players contest the football.
The defensive crumber establishes front-and-centre position before the ball arrives.
The attacking crumber attempts to win the spill and score.
The goal-side defender protects any football spilling behind the contest.
If the defensive crumber wins possession, they select an appropriate exit gate.
Defenders score one point for neutralising the attacking crumb and two points for winning and exiting.
Reset after each possession.
coachingPoints: Move into front-and-centre position while the football is in flight.
Stay goal-side of the attacking crumber.
Avoid being drawn directly under the marking contest.
Read the likely direction of the spoil.
Use legal body positioning to protect the drop zone.
Keep the hands free and remain ready to collect at ground level.
If possession cannot be won, prevent the attacker from escaping centrally.
Communicate with the aerial and goal-side defenders.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the defensive crumber moves before the spill occurs.
Whether goal-side position is maintained.
Whether the player remains balanced at ground level.
Whether the attacking crumber gains a central exit.
Whether the deeper defender protects the back of the contest.
Whether the defensive exit suits the pressure.

commonErrors.error: Defensive crumber stands directly under the aerial players.
commonErrors.correction: Position several metres front and centre of the contest.

commonErrors.error: Attacking crumber gains inside position.
commonErrors.correction: Recover goal-side and use legal body positioning before the spill.

commonErrors.error: Defender waits for the football to hit the ground.
commonErrors.correction: Read the kick and spoil direction while the ball is in flight.

commonErrors.error: Defender tries to pick up under immediate pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Knock the football to support or create a stoppage when clean possession is unavailable.

progressions: Add a second attacking crumber.
Vary the location of the aerial contest.
Introduce full body contact.
Allow the attacking crumber to begin from either side.
Add a second defensive possession after the first exit.
regressions: Use a coach-controlled drop rather than a kick.
Give the defensive crumber a positional head start.
successIndicators: Establish front-and-centre position early.
Remain goal-side of the attacking crumber.
Read and attack the likely spill.
Deny a clean central scoring opportunity.
Win, neutralise or safely exit the ground ball.
matchApplication: Forward crumbers are most dangerous when positioned front and centre of a marking contest. Defenders must protect this area before the spill occurs and prevent the opposition from gathering cleanly towards goal.
relatedDrills: TD-016 – Protecting the Top of Defensive 50

title: Pressure the Receiver on Arrival
primarySkill: Closing a receiver as possession arrives to prevent forward continuation.
objective: Develop defenders’ ability to arrive with controlled pressure as an opponent receives possession, preventing the receiver from turning, accelerating or disposing effectively.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations and several observable behaviours
setup:
Mark a rectangular area with a target gate at each end.
Position a feeder with two possible receivers ahead.
Place a defender three to five metres from each receiver.
Receivers may lead forward, laterally or back towards the feeder.
Defenders begin goal-side and must read the feeder’s disposal.
Rotate feeding, attacking and defending roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receivers move to create a passing option.
The feeder selects one receiver and disposes by kick or handball.
The defender closes while the football is travelling.
The defender aims to arrive as possession is taken.
If the receiver plays on, controlled tackling becomes live.
The receiver attempts to move through the target gate or release to the second attacker.
Defenders score one point for forcing a backwards disposal and two points for a turnover.
Reset with receivers changing starting positions.
coachingPoints: Read the feeder’s body position before the disposal.
Begin closing as the football is released.
Arrive close enough to prevent the receiver turning.
Decelerate during the final steps.
Maintain goal-side position.
Close the receiver’s preferred disposal side.
Do not make early contact before possession is established.
Recover immediately if the receiver releases the football.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders read the disposal early.
Whether closing begins during the football’s travel.
Whether players arrive balanced.
Whether receivers are prevented from turning forward.
Whether pressure influences the next disposal.
Whether defenders continue after the ball is released.

commonErrors.error: Defender waits until possession is completed.
commonErrors.correction: Move as soon as the feeder commits to the disposal.

commonErrors.error: Defender arrives too fast and overruns.
commonErrors.correction: Shorten the final steps and decelerate before contact.

commonErrors.error: Defender allows the receiver to turn inside.
commonErrors.correction: Close from the goal-side and protect the central route.

commonErrors.error: Defender contacts before the mark or possession.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain legal pressure and contest only when permitted.

progressions: Add a third receiver.
Allow the feeder to use longer kicks.
Introduce full tackling after play on.
Reduce the defender’s starting distance.
Continue play through multiple consecutive receivers.
successIndicators: Read the disposal before it arrives.
Close during the football’s travel.
Arrive balanced and legally.
Prevent receivers from turning forward.
Force sideways, backwards or ineffective disposals.
matchApplication: Defensive pressure is most effective when it arrives with the football. Closing late allows opponents to turn and accelerate, while arriving under control can stop forward momentum and force a predictable disposal.

title: Contest-to-Contest Defensive Repeat
primarySkill: Reorganising and applying pressure across consecutive contests.
objective: Develop players’ ability to complete one defensive contest, recover immediately and establish pressure, cover and balance around the next contest.
groundSize: 50 metres long × 35 metres wide, divided into three contest zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Divide the area into three consecutive contest zones.
Position attackers and defenders in each zone.
Begin with a ground-ball or aerial contest in the first zone.
The coach holds spare footballs to initiate the next phase.
After each contest, selected defenders must move forward or fold behind into the next zone.
Rotate players through all three zones.
howTheDrillWorks:
The first contest begins from a coach-directed football.
Once possession is resolved, the coach immediately starts a second contest in the next zone.
Defenders from the completed contest recover and join the next phase.
The nearest player becomes pressure, the second provides cover and the third holds balance.
A third contest begins immediately after the second phase.
Defenders score one point for each stopped attack and three points for winning all three phases.
Attackers score by exiting through the final gate.
Complete work blocks of 45–60 seconds before rotating.
coachingPoints: Do not remain at a completed contest.
Recover through the shortest useful route.
Identify the next pressure, cover and balance roles while moving.
Communicate which defenders are arriving.
Avoid having every player chase the football.
Maintain legal contact technique under fatigue.
Fold behind when the next contest moves away.
Finish each phase before preparing to exit.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders react immediately to the next contest.
Whether recovery routes are efficient.
Whether roles are established before arrival.
Whether defensive structure survives repeated effort.
Whether players communicate while fatigued.
Whether contact remains controlled and legal.

commonErrors.error: Defenders remain at the previous contest.
commonErrors.correction: Turn immediately and identify the next dangerous phase.

commonErrors.error: Everyone arrives as a pressure player.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate pressure, cover and balance while recovering.

commonErrors.error: Players run through congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Fold behind the contest through clear goal-side space.

commonErrors.error: Technique deteriorates under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Decelerate before contact and maintain body control.

progressions: Reduce time between contests.
Use full match-like contact.
Add a fourth contest phase.
Begin each phase from an unpredictable location.
Require a controlled exit after the final defensive win.
successIndicators: Leave completed contests immediately.
Recover through effective routes.
Establish new defensive roles quickly.
Maintain structure across repeated phases.
Complete several defensive efforts without losing discipline.
matchApplication: Australian football regularly involves several contests in rapid succession. Defenders must leave completed actions, recover around the football and contribute to the next phase before the opposition can escape.
relatedDrills: TD-029 – Defensive Fold Around the Contest
TD-040 – Defensive Movement Under Fatigue Assessment

title: Advanced Pressure and Contest Assessment
primarySkill: Applying advanced defensive pressure and contest principles during continuous match-like play.
objective: Assess whether players can independently combine the advanced pressure and contest behaviours developed through TD-051 to TD-059 across changing field positions and repeated phases.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two-thirds or the full ground.
Divide players into attacking and defending teams.
Prepare the following starting scenarios:
Ball carrier under tackle pressure with a nearby release
Loose ground ball with outside support
Pressured kick into an intercept channel
Aerial contest requiring a directional spoil
Attacking crumb inside 50
Boundary stoppage
Repeat forward entries
Position coaches to assess pressure, cover, balance, communication and legal contact.
Rotate teams after completing all scenarios.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins each repetition from one prepared scenario.
The attacking team attempts to retain possession, exit or score.
The defence must apply the correct pressure and contest response without prior instruction.
All spills, smothers, tackles and spoils remain live.
If the attacking team retains possession, the phase continues into another contest.
After winning possession, defenders attempt a controlled exit.
Each repetition lasts 60–120 seconds.
Complete six to eight repetitions before exchanging roles.
coachingPoints: Decide whether the second defender should assist the tackle or protect the release.
Compress around ground balls without losing outside balance.
Use pressure to shape opposition disposals.
Direct spoils away from goal and towards support.
Pressure attacking crumbers immediately.
Close receivers as possession arrives.
Reorganise between consecutive contests.
Protect the corridor at boundary stoppages.
Reset after repeated forward entries.
Maintain safe, legal and disciplined contact.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether tackle assistance is used appropriately.
Whether release lanes remain protected.
Whether the defence retains balance around ground-ball contests.
Whether pressure influences kicks and handballs.
Whether spoils are directed towards safe space.
Whether crumbers and receivers are pressured immediately.
Whether players recover into the next contest.
Whether boundary exits are denied.
Whether repeated entries are defended with structure.
Whether defensive wins lead to composed exits.

commonErrors.error: Multiple defenders commit to one contest.
commonErrors.correction: Retain clear pressure, release-cover and balance responsibilities.

commonErrors.error: Pressure is applied without influencing the disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Close from an angle that removes the dangerous option.

commonErrors.error: Players watch spoils or loose footballs develop.
commonErrors.correction: Move into the expected second-ball area before the contest finishes.

commonErrors.error: Repeated defensive efforts become unstructured.
commonErrors.correction: Reset roles and goal-side positioning after every phase.

commonErrors.error: Contact technique deteriorates under fatigue.
commonErrors.correction: Decelerate before contact and maintain legal tackling and bodywork.

progressions: Remove all coach explanation before each scenario.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure consequences.
Begin scenarios from unpredictable turnovers.
Require the defensive exit to develop into a complete forward entry.
Allow the attacking team to select and repeat the scenario it believes can expose the defence.
regressions: Assess one scenario at a time.
Use controlled rather than match-like contact.
Allow defensive organisation before each restart.
Shorten the work periods and increase recovery.
successIndicators: Apply the correct pressure response to each scenario.
Protect release options while contesting possession.
Maintain balance around ground balls and tackles.
Influence opposition disposals towards defensive support.
Control aerial and ground-level spills.
Complete repeated defensive actions.
Communicate throughout congested and open phases.
Preserve legal contact technique under fatigue.
Win possession and complete an appropriate exit.
Adapt without constant coach direction.
matchApplication: This assessment combines the advanced pressure and contest behaviours required throughout Australian football. It measures whether players can create turnovers through coordinated tackling, ground-ball pressure, influenced disposals, controlled spoiling and repeat defensive effort while preserving the wider team structure.

title: Defensive Reset After Opposition Switch Mark
Team Defence Structure and Adaptability Assessment
Must-Regain Full-Ground Press
primarySkill: Applying an aggressive full-ground press when immediate possession regain is required.
objective: Develop the coordinated high-risk defensive pressure required when the team must regain possession quickly to create a late scoring opportunity.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Set the pressing team seven points behind with two minutes remaining.
Begin with the opposition taking a kick-in or holding possession in defensive 50.
Assign direct opponents across the ground.
Retain one deeper balance defender behind the highest pressure line.
Mark one central and two wide opposition exit gates.
Nominate one pressure caller in each line.
Position a coach near the scoreboard to update time.
howTheDrillWorks:
The opposition attempts to retain possession and run down the clock.
The pressing team applies close accountability and aggressive pressure.
The nearest defender pressures the ball carrier while teammates deny short uncontested options.
Players behind the press step forward to reduce usable space.
The team may leave a low-value long contest available while removing easy possession.
After regaining the football, the pressing team attacks goal immediately but with organised support.
If the opposition exits through a gate, the press must recover and re-establish further up the ground.
The repetition ends when time expires, the pressing team levels the score or the opposition retains possession for 40 seconds.
coachingPoints: Understand that greater defensive risk is justified by the scoreboard.
Maintain direct accountability on short options.
Pressure the ball carrier’s preferred side.
Compress every line behind the first pressure action.
Retain limited protection against a long escape.
Communicate switches and screens immediately.
Avoid conceding uncontested marks that consume time.
After a regain, create a scoring opportunity before the opposition resets.
Maintain legal tackling and marking pressure.
Do not confuse aggressive defence with several players chasing the same opponent.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players recognise the need for increased risk.
Whether short options are directly accountable.
Whether the first possession is pressured.
Whether midfield and backline players step behind the press.
Whether a deep safety position remains.
Whether defenders communicate opponent exchanges.
Whether the regain produces an organised attack.
Whether fatigue affects legal contact technique.

commonErrors.error: Players use a passive zone despite needing possession.
commonErrors.correction: Move into direct accountability and deny uncontested short options.

commonErrors.error: Several defenders chase the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Keep one pressure player while others close likely receivers.

commonErrors.error: No protection remains behind the press.
commonErrors.correction: Retain one deeper balance defender against the long escape.

commonErrors.error: Players win possession but rush a blind disposal.
commonErrors.correction: Attack quickly with a visible target and support underneath.

commonErrors.error: Defenders concede uncontested marks near the boundary.
commonErrors.correction: Close the receiver as the football travels and force a contest.

progressions: Reduce the remaining time to 60 seconds.
Increase the deficit to 11 points.
Begin with the opposition already holding an uncontested mark.
Remove the nominated pressure callers.
Allow the opposition to use deliberate switches and backwards possession.
Continue immediately after a score with a centre-bounce scenario.
regressions: Give the pressing team a numerical advantage.
Allow defensive organisation before each restart.
successIndicators: Apply direct pressure to short possession.
Compress the full-ground structure.
Deny uncontested clock-consuming marks.
Preserve limited cover behind the press.
Create a turnover within the available time.
Convert the regain into a realistic scoring opportunity.
Maintain discipline despite increased defensive aggression.
matchApplication: When trailing late, normal containment may not create possession quickly enough. The team must accept greater risk, close short options and force the opposition into contested or hurried disposals.
relatedDrills: TD-063 – Forward-Line Press with Behind-Ball Cover

title: Final-Ninety-Seconds Boundary Defence
primarySkill: Managing boundary-side defence and stoppages during the final stages of a close match.
objective: Develop players’ ability to use the boundary, control stoppages and make disciplined defensive decisions during the final 90 seconds of a close match.
groundSize: One boundary-side half of the ground from the centre wing to the goal line.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Set the defending team five points ahead with 90 seconds remaining.
Begin with the opposition in possession near the boundary at half-forward.
Position players for a likely boundary contest or stoppage.
Nominate a score-and-time communicator.
Establish the applicable stoppage and boundary restart rules for the playing group.
Run repeated scenarios from marks, throw-ins, ground balls and free kicks.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team attempts to score before time expires.
The defence protects the inside route and directs possession towards the boundary.
At boundary stoppages, defenders protect the corridor-side exit.
If the defence wins possession, players decide whether to retain, advance along the boundary or take a safe mark.
If the football leaves the area, the coach restarts with the appropriate scenario and adjusts the clock.
Deliberate illegal time wasting results in a turnover or free kick to the attack.
The attacking team receives an immediate repeat entry after a rushed central defensive turnover.
The repetition ends when time expires, the score changes or the defence establishes secure possession.
coachingPoints: Know the score and remaining time.
Protect the corridor side of every boundary contest.
Use the boundary without relying on illegal or reckless actions.
Maintain one defender behind the immediate contest.
Prevent the attacking team from releasing backwards into central space.
Communicate stoppage roles before the restart.
After winning possession, select a legal low-risk option.
Avoid taking the football into unnecessary central congestion.
Remain prepared for the opposition to switch quickly.
Do not concede avoidable free kicks through undisciplined contact.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players understand the match situation.
Whether the inside stoppage exit is protected.
Whether a deeper balance player remains.
Whether contact remains legal.
Whether the defence uses the boundary intelligently.
Whether players communicate restart roles.
Whether possession decisions suit the clock.
Whether the team remains alert to a switch.
Whether the defence avoids unnecessary free kicks.

commonErrors.error: Defenders attack from the boundary side and open the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Position inside and force possession towards the line.

commonErrors.error: Every defender enters the stoppage.
commonErrors.correction: Retain inside cover and one deeper balance player.

commonErrors.error: Players attempt illegal time wasting.
commonErrors.correction: Use lawful possession, marks and boundary movement.

commonErrors.error: A defensive win is kicked blindly into central space.
commonErrors.correction: Secure the football and choose a controlled boundary or support option.

commonErrors.error: Defenders become unaware of a switch.
commonErrors.correction: Keep weak-side communication and scan beyond the immediate contest.

progressions: Reduce the lead to one point.
Begin with 45 seconds remaining.
Start from a defensive free kick near the boundary.
Give the attacking team an extra player.
Remove visible clock updates.
Begin after the opposition scores a behind and the defence must take a kick-in.
regressions: Allow defensive organisation before each restart.
Pause after possession changes to discuss the decision.
successIndicators: Communicate score and time.
Protect the inside route at boundary contests.
Use the boundary legally and effectively.
Maintain defensive balance around stoppages.
Avoid undisciplined free kicks.
Select safe possession options.
Prevent a high-value central scoring opportunity.
preserve the lead until time expires.
matchApplication: The final stages of close matches demand precise tactical and legal decision making. Boundary control, stoppage organisation and possession security can prevent the opposition from gaining the central access required for a winning score.

title: Player-Led Defensive Command Chain
primarySkill: Organising and adapting team defence through player-led communication.
objective: Develop players’ ability to lead the defensive structure, communicate tactical changes and solve emerging match problems without direct coach instruction.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Arrange both teams in realistic structures.
Nominate one leader in the forward line, midfield and backline.
Give only the attacking team the initial scenario information.
Possible attacking plans include:
Repeated switches
Corridor handball chain
Long down-the-line exit
Isolated key forward
Possession retention
Numerical overload
The coach remains silent during each playing phase.
Defensive leaders may call “match”, “zone”, “press”, “drop”, “delay” or “release”.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins using its selected plan.
Defensive players identify the attacking method through live play.
Unit leaders communicate information through the forward, midfield and backline.
A defensive system is selected and applied.
Leaders may change the structure as the attacking method evolves.
Players outside formal leadership roles contribute local information and confirm responsibilities.
After winning possession, the defence transitions while retaining turnover protection.
The coach reviews the communication and decisions only after the phase ends.
coachingPoints: Leaders must communicate what is happening, not merely demand greater effort.
Calls should include the problem, system and immediate action.
Information must travel through every line.
The deepest players communicate space and opponents behind the structure.
The nearest players communicate pressure and immediate options.
Confirm responsibility after every tactical change.
Avoid conflicting calls from several leaders.
Change the system when the original solution is no longer suitable.
Non-leaders must acknowledge and support instructions.
Maintain calm, specific communication during high-pressure phases.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether players recognise the attacking method.
Whether leaders communicate early.
Whether calls are specific and actionable.
Whether information reaches all defensive lines.
Whether teammates acknowledge instructions.
Whether the selected defensive system suits the problem.
Whether leaders change the structure when required.
Whether local communication supports the broader system.
Whether conflicting calls are resolved.
Whether the team remains organised without coach intervention.

commonErrors.error: Leaders provide vague encouragement only.
commonErrors.correction: Name the tactical problem and required action.

commonErrors.error: Different lines use different systems.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm one team-wide call and repeat it through every unit.

commonErrors.error: Players wait for formal leaders to identify local opponents.
commonErrors.correction: Everyone must communicate immediate threats and responsibilities.

commonErrors.error: Leaders continue with an ineffective structure.
commonErrors.correction: Reassess after each attacking success and change the system when required.

commonErrors.error: Too many players issue conflicting commands.
commonErrors.correction: Give priority to the player with the clearest view and confirm the final call.

progressions: Remove nominated leaders.
Change the attacking plan during the phase.
Add scoreboard and time-pressure information.
Use full match-like contact.
Allow the attack to conceal its plan until play begins.
Continue through extended uninterrupted match simulation.
regressions: Tell defensive leaders the attacking plan.
Pause once during the phase for player organisation.
Allow the coach to ask guiding questions between disposals.
successIndicators: Recognise attacking patterns.
Communicate the tactical problem clearly.
Select an appropriate defensive response.
Transfer information through every line.
Confirm individual responsibilities.
Adapt the structure during live play.
Remain organised without coach direction.
Transition after defensive wins without losing balance.
matchApplication: Coaches cannot direct every defensive adjustment during a match. Successful teams rely on players who can recognise attacking patterns, communicate solutions and organise teammates while play continues.

title: Defensive Wing Fold and Corridor Screen
primarySkill: Using the defensive-side wing to fold behind possession and protect the corridor.
objective: Develop the defensive wing’s ability to narrow behind the football, screen central movement, support long contests and expand again when possession changes sides.
groundSize: Two-thirds of the ground using the full width.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position the attacking team with possession on one wing.
Arrange defenders across forward, midfield and backline units.
Nominate one defender on the opposite wing as the defensive folding wing.
Place attacking gates through the corridor and both wings.
Establish a likely long-kick contest on the ball side.
Place two defensive rebound gates on the opposite side.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attack moves possession along one side of the ground.
The defensive-side wing narrows behind the football into a corridor-screening position.
If the attack kicks long down the line, the wing folds behind the contest to provide cover or ground-level support.
If the attack switches, the wing expands towards the new receiver while another teammate assumes the central screen.
The wing communicates runners entering from behind.
Defenders score one point for denying the corridor, two points for winning the long contest and three points for rebounding through the opposite gate.
The attack scores three points for a clean corridor break.
Rotate wing and midfield roles after each block.
coachingPoints: The defensive wing should narrow when the football is on the opposite side.
Protect the corridor without becoming so narrow that the wide switch is uncontested.
Move before the ball carrier disposes.
Fold behind the expected long contest rather than arriving level with it.
Identify forwards and midfielders running into central space.
Communicate who replaces the corridor-screening position when expanding.
Retain goal-side movement during switches.
Support the first defensive possession after the turnover.
Expand quickly after possession is secured.
Avoid standing stationary between opponents without affecting a passing lane.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the wing narrows early enough.
Whether the corridor passing lane is genuinely affected.
Whether the wing reaches the back of long contests.
Whether the far-side switch remains defendable.
Whether replacement cover is communicated.
Whether late runners are identified.
Whether the wing supports the defensive rebound.

commonErrors.error: Defensive wing remains on the boundary away from play.
commonErrors.correction: Narrow into a central screening position behind the football.

commonErrors.error: Wing moves directly towards the contest and arrives in front.
commonErrors.correction: Fold around the back to provide goal-side cover.

commonErrors.error: The switch is completed before the wing reacts.
commonErrors.correction: Read the ball carrier’s preparation and expand while the kick travels.

commonErrors.error: No teammate replaces the central screen.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate the rotation before moving towards the new ball side.

commonErrors.error: Wing wins possession but disposes without support.
commonErrors.correction: Connect with the nearest midfield or half-back outlet.

progressions: Remove the nominated folding wing.
Allow repeated switches.
Add full match-like tackling.
Begin from rapid turnovers.
Add a second long contest after the initial rebound.
Use full-ground positional structures.
regressions: Mark the folding wing’s reference position.
Allow the coach to call fold and expand movements.
successIndicators: Narrow behind possession.
Protect central passing lanes.
Support the back of long contests.
Expand in time to pressure switches.
Communicate replacement responsibilities.
Connect with teammates after the defensive win.
matchApplication: The wing away from the football plays an important defensive role by protecting the corridor, supporting contests and preventing the opposition from moving directly through the centre. The role changes quickly when possession switches sides.
relatedDrills: TD-005 – Ball-Side Pressure and Weak-Side Cover
TD-029 – Defensive Fold Around the Contest

title: Half-Back Intercept-to-Outlet Unit
primarySkill: Connecting half-back intercept positioning with a reliable first outlet.
objective: Develop a half-back unit that influences the forward entry, wins possession and immediately connects with a safe supporting outlet.
groundSize: From the centre square to the goal line.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Arrange three to five half-back defenders across the top and inside defensive 50.
Position attackers across half-forward and inside 50.
Place one defensive midfielder in front of the half-back line.
Position two outlet players towards the wings.
Mark one central and two wide outlet gates.
Begin each repetition with the attack controlling possession across half-forward.
howTheDrillWorks:
The midfield defender pressures or screens the forward-entry options.
Half-backs adjust depth according to the pressure on the ball carrier.
One defender attacks the likely entry while teammates protect underneath and behind.
If the defence intercepts or wins the spill, the nearest outlet players create width.
The interceptor selects a short release, wide switch or controlled central connection.
The remaining half-backs retain turnover protection behind the first outlet.
Defenders score two points for the intercept and an additional point for a successful supported outlet.
The attack receives a repeat entry if the first outlet turns over.
coachingPoints: Entry pressure and intercept positioning must work together.
The interceptor should hold enough depth to attack the football moving forward.
Supporting half-backs protect short and ground-level options.
Outlet players must move as possession is being won.
The interceptor should scan before completing the mark or collection.
Avoid every defender spreading ahead of the football.
Use a short outlet when it removes pressure.
Use width when the corridor is congested.
Central rebound should be selected only when support and field position make it safe.
Rebuild defensive shape immediately after an unsuccessful outlet.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether entry pressure influences the attacking disposal.
Whether intercept defenders position at useful depth.
Whether teammates protect underneath the intercept.
Whether outlets move before possession is secured.
Whether the first disposal suits the pressure.
Whether turnover protection remains.
Whether the unit resets after a failed rebound.

commonErrors.error: Half-back stands directly beside the forward.
commonErrors.correction: Create intercept separation while maintaining opponent awareness.

commonErrors.error: Outlet players wait until the intercept is completed.
commonErrors.correction: Move during the flight of the entry kick.

commonErrors.error: Every defender runs forward after possession is won.
commonErrors.correction: Retain at least one player behind the rebound.

commonErrors.error: Interceptor immediately kicks long under little pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Use the free short outlet to secure the transition.

commonErrors.error: Failed outlet leaves the backline disorganised.
commonErrors.correction: Recover goal-side and rebuild line connection immediately.

progressions: Add full match-like contact.
Allow the attack to switch before entering.
Add a second forward entry after a failed outlet.
Remove marked outlet gates.
Require the rebound to progress into a forward entry.
Introduce scoreboard scenarios affecting the outlet decision.
successIndicators: Influence and read the forward entry.
Position to intercept moving towards the football.
Protect the ground-level contest.
Create immediate supporting outlets.
Select a first disposal appropriate to the pressure.
Retain cover behind the rebound.
Reset quickly after an unsuccessful exit.
matchApplication: Half-backs are not only responsible for winning intercept possession. The quality of the first outlet determines whether the defensive win becomes a controlled transition or another opposition entry.

title: Midfield Stoppage Sweep and Cover
primarySkill: Positioning a defensive midfielder behind a stoppage to protect the opposition’s forward exit.
objective: Develop the defensive sweep role behind stoppages so the midfield can pressure the first possession, protect the forward release and connect with the backline.
groundSize: Centre-square or midfield stoppage area measuring approximately 45 metres × 40 metres.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Establish a central stoppage with ruck and midfield players.
Place three attacking exit gates forward, left and right.
Nominate one defender as the midfield sweep player behind the stoppage.
Position a half-back defender deeper as the next protective layer.
The attacking team may win possession through the front, side or back of the stoppage.
Rotate sweep, inside-midfield and half-back roles.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with a ball-up, throw-in simulation or ground-ball stoppage.
Inside defenders pressure the first possession.
The sweep player positions goal-side of the likely forward exit.
If the football leaves through the front of the stoppage, the sweep player pressures, tackles or intercepts.
If possession exits laterally, the sweep player adjusts while maintaining central protection.
The deeper defender communicates runners moving beyond the sweep.
After winning possession, the defence connects through a rebound gate.
The defence scores for stopping the forward exit, recovering the spill and completing the first connection.
coachingPoints: The sweep player must begin goal-side of the stoppage.
Position close enough to affect the first clean exit but not so close that congestion removes vision.
Read ruck positioning and the body shape of inside midfielders.
Protect the forward and corridor-side release first.
Communicate with the deeper half-back line.
Do not become drawn into every ground-ball contest.
If the first exit is lateral, adjust without surrendering the centre.
Attack loose footballs moving forward.
After the turnover, provide or use the first safe midfield connection.
Rotate the sweep role when the stoppage moves.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether the sweep player starts goal-side.
Whether the first forward exit is pressured.
Whether the player remains outside unnecessary congestion.
Whether lateral movement opens the corridor.
Whether communication connects midfield and half-back.
Whether the sweep player attacks loose possession.
Whether the first rebound disposal is supported.

commonErrors.error: Sweep player stands level with the stoppage.
commonErrors.correction: Begin behind the contest and protect the forward exit.

commonErrors.error: Player becomes trapped inside congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Hold enough separation to scan and close the release.

commonErrors.error: Lateral possession draws the sweep away from the corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust while maintaining central protection.

commonErrors.error: No communication occurs with half-backs.
commonErrors.correction: Identify runners and the next layer before the stoppage begins.

commonErrors.error: Sweep player wins possession and kicks blindly.
commonErrors.correction: Connect with the nearest available support option.

progressions: Add an attacking midfielder beginning behind the sweep.
Allow unrestricted stoppage exits.
Introduce full match-like tackling.
Move the stoppage to the wing and half-forward.
Add a second stoppage immediately after the first possession.
Continue a defensive regain into full-ground transition.
regressions: Pause after the first possession to assess positioning.
successIndicators: Establish goal-side sweep position.
Protect the opposition’s forward stoppage exit.
Remain connected to the half-back line.
Avoid unnecessary congestion.
Pressure, intercept or recover the first release.
Connect effectively after the defensive win.
matchApplication: A defensive midfielder positioned behind the stoppage can prevent one clean clearance from exposing the backline. The role requires disciplined spacing, scanning and connection rather than simply joining the initial contest.

title: High-Forward Exit Denial Rotation
primarySkill: Rotating high forwards between ball pressure, short-outlet denial and long-contest coverage.
objective: Develop a coordinated high-forward unit that adjusts its responsibilities as the opposition changes between short exits, switches and long kicks.
groundSize: From the opposition goal line to the centre square.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert management of complex scenarios, multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Position the opposition to begin from a kick-in or defensive possession.
Arrange three to five high forwards across the first defensive line.
Position midfield support behind the forwards.
Mark one central and two wide opposition exit gates.
Identify three rotating high-forward roles:
Ball-pressure player
Short-outlet defender
Long-contest support
Rotate players through each role.
howTheDrillWorks:
The opposition begins its exit from defensive 50.
The nearest high forward applies pressure to the ball carrier.
The second high forward protects the most dangerous short outlet.
The third forward positions to affect the likely long kick or second possession.
When the ball moves, the forwards rotate into new pressure, outlet and contest roles.
Midfielders compress behind the high-forward line.
The pressing team scores for forcing a hurried long kick, creating a turnover or regaining possession inside 50.
The opposition scores for an uncontested corridor exit.
coachingPoints: High forwards must defend as a unit rather than chase individually.
The ball-pressure player closes from the corridor side where possible.
The short-outlet defender arrives as the receiver takes possession.
The long-contest player must position before the kick is released.
Rotate roles immediately after each disposal.
Maintain connection with the midfield screen.
Do not allow all forwards to become trapped near the ball.
Recognise when the opposition has broken the first line and recover centrally.
After a regain, create width and scoring support.
Maintain legal pressure around marks and kick-ins.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether all three high-forward roles are occupied.
Whether short receivers are closed as possession arrives.
Whether the long kick is anticipated.
Whether roles rotate after each disposal.
Whether midfield support remains connected.
Whether several forwards chase the same possession.
Whether players recover after the first line is broken.

commonErrors.error: Every forward pressures the ball carrier.
commonErrors.correction: Retain separate short-outlet and long-contest responsibilities.

commonErrors.error: The short receiver is allowed to turn.
commonErrors.correction: Close while the football is travelling.

commonErrors.error: Long-contest coverage reacts after the kick.
commonErrors.correction: Position before the ball carrier completes the disposal.

commonErrors.error: Midfield remains too deep behind the press.
commonErrors.correction: Compress towards the expected second possession.

commonErrors.error: High forwards stop after being bypassed.
commonErrors.correction: Recover through the corridor and reconnect with midfield.

progressions: Allow rapid play-on kick-ins.
Remove nominated roles.
Add repeated opposition switches.
Introduce full match-like tackling.
Add scoreboard scenarios requiring higher or lower defensive risk.
Continue the regain into a complete scoring phase.
regressions: Use one side of the ground.
Allow the forwards to set before each restart.
successIndicators: Fill the pressure, outlet and long-contest roles.
Rotate responsibilities as possession moves.
Deny uncontested short exits.
Influence or contest the long kick.
Remain connected with midfield support.
Recover when the first defensive line is broken.
Convert regains into organised attacking opportunities.
matchApplication: High forwards begin the team’s defensive structure. Their ability to rotate between pressure, short-outlet denial and long-contest support determines whether the opposition exits cleanly or is forced into predictable possession.
relatedDrills: TD-063 – Forward-Line Press with Behind-Ball Cover

title: Wet-Weather Territory Defence
primarySkill: Defending territory and ground-level possession under wet-weather conditions.
objective: Develop a defensive method suited to wet conditions in which players protect central territory, expect imperfect possession and prevent dangerous ground-level exits.
groundSize: Two-thirds of the ground, with selected boundary-side contest zones.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use damp footballs to simulate reduced handling reliability without deliberately creating an unsafe surface.
Mark central high-risk territory and two wider low-risk channels.
Position teams in realistic structures.
Establish several ground-ball and aerial-contest starting points.
Place territorial target zones near the boundary and away from goal.
Check footing and reduce contact intensity if the surface becomes unsafe.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins with an aerial kick, bouncing football or contested ground ball.
The attacking team attempts to move centrally and score.
Defenders protect the corridor and force possession towards wider territory.
Around loose footballs, the nearest player pressures while teammates protect the release.
Aerial defenders spoil towards the boundary or support rather than back towards goal.
If defenders cannot secure clean possession, they may knock or kick the football towards a territorial target zone.
Defenders score for forcing the football wide, creating a stoppage in safe territory or completing a controlled exit.
The attack receives bonus points for clean central possession after a defensive handling error.
coachingPoints: Expect the football to spill and position for the second possession.
Protect central territory before attempting low-percentage possession.
Use the boundary as a defensive support.
Stay on the feet around ground-ball contests where practical.
Avoid unnecessary short handballs in heavy congestion.
Spoil and knock the football towards safe territory.
Maintain one player outside congestion for the release or next spill.
Communicate the safest direction before the contest.
Secure possession with body protection when a clean gather is available.
Adjust contact and speed to the safety of the conditions.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Whether defenders protect central territory.
Whether players anticipate handling errors and spills.
Whether all defenders collapse into congestion.
Whether aerial spoils move away from goal.
Whether disposal choices suit the conditions.
Whether players maintain safe balance and contact.
Whether the team accepts stoppages in favourable territory.

commonErrors.error: Defenders attempt difficult clean gathers in heavy congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Knock the football towards support or safer territory when possession is unlikely.

commonErrors.error: Players use repeated short handballs around a slippery contest.
commonErrors.correction: Use a direct territorial disposal or create a stoppage.

commonErrors.error: Spoils return towards the corridor or goal.
commonErrors.correction: Direct the football towards the boundary or defensive support.

commonErrors.error: Every defender enters the ground-ball contest.
commonErrors.correction: Retain release-lane and outside-balance players.

commonErrors.error: Intensity remains unchanged on an unsafe surface.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce contact and movement speed or relocate the drill.

progressions: Introduce changing wind direction.
Begin from repeated inside-50 entries.
Add match-like contact where conditions are safe.
Use scoreboard scenarios requiring territory protection.
